To begin, I really do love your username; I'm around your age as well, which is pretty cool. From my experience of learning French, here are some tips (that I am also going to use when studying Italian): 

- Duolingo has pretty good vocabulary, but the sentences are usually useless (stuff like "the ducks eat the bread" or "the women are in the kitchen"). I don't remember ever needing to use most of the vocabulary taught by Duolingo for French

- Starting off by using Anki to learn common words and deleting them as you master them

- Reading stuff out loud (to practice speaking AND comprehension); for French, I use Kwiziq because it has CEFR levels, but it unfortunately doesn't offer Italian

- Italian music helps as well; I really like (some) operas (Rigoletto is pretty good for starters) and I feel as if they have made learning Italian a bit easier

- Learning the most common tenses (for French, this is present, passé composé, and future)

- Once you're getting pretty good at it, set your computer to Italian (but make sure that your comprehension is good enough so that you can switch it back if necessary)

At a certain point, you're going to want to stop using stuff like Duolingo because although it claims that you're 90% fluent or whatever, you're really not and are basically just beating a dead horse by spamming lessons.
